newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems protest NATO blockade of frontline village.
newsitem.headline: Moslems protest NATO blockade of frontline village.

text.p: Several hundred protestors gathered at Tuzla airbase on Monday demanding an end to what they said was NATO peackeepers' blockade of a village in Serb-held northeast Bosnia recently resettled by Moslems.
The protestors carried banners saying: "We want to go home. You made a promise, so take us back" and "IFOR, protect people, don't torture them".
IFOR is the acronym for the 60,000 NATO-led peacekeeping force which deployed in Bosnia last December to monitor the Dayton peace treaty which halted almost four years of fighting.
Russian troops serving with IFOR monitor northeast Bosnia, where the disputed village of Jusici lies, along with some 20,000 U.S. troops.
"Russians: Grozny, Jusici, what is next?" another banner said.
Protestors said a much larger protest, possibly blocking the airbase, would be staged on Tuesday.

More than 100 men, claiming to be former residents of Jusici, crossed former frontlines ten days ago and returned to the village to reclaim their homes. Some of them carried weapons, in clear violation of the Dayton treaty.
After disarming the returnees IFOR asked them to go back to the federation territory and come back with proper paperwork on residence and ownership.
Local Serb police showed uncharacteristic restraint, waiting for the stand-off to be resolved.
The number of people swelled when more women and children showed up in the burnt out village.
Russian peacekeepers then boosted their presence in the remote village to keep the Moslems in and the Serbs out, in order to avoid an open conflict of former enemies.
A government relief official in Tuzla told Reuters rations of food and water in Jusici were scant and there was no medical help.

"The first teams entered only yesterday and the situation this morning was quite alarming. Many are suffering from diarrhoea, many children have a cold," said Fadil Banjanovic, of Tuzla office for the return of refugees.
NATO warned on Monday the Moslem occupation of villages in the Serb territory could be a mask for a military motive.

"The villages are a few kilometres from the Drina river. It doesn't take a genius to figure they could be jumping-off points for an army effort one day to cut the Serb republic in half," said a NATO officer who asked not to be named.
The Bosnian government says there was no ulterior motive behind a natural desire by refugees to return to their homes.
The Dayton treaty, while advocating freedom of movement for everyone, has turned former front lines into a de facto border between Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and its Serb republic.
Although Dayton guaranteed refugees displaced by the war the right to return to their homes, only a few hundred, most of them Moslems, have risked crossing ethnic boundary lines.
